articles.title: A-listers and AI stylists: how high-street brands are staging a fashion comeback
articles.summary: Gap, M&S, Topshop and more are taking a leaf from luxury label playbooks to satisfy savvier generation of shoppers. High street brands that boomed in the noughties before the squeeze of both sustainably minded consumers and the rise of ultra-cheap online labels are staging a comeback.
body: This time, rather than focusing solely on trend-led affordable designs, the names familiar to any shopper are courting luxury fashion, A-list collaborations and enhanced services in an attempt to engage consumers.

Think Gap’s new collection with Victoria Beckham. Or Marks & Spencer showcasing a covetable catwalk collection at London fashion week with celebrities including Joan Collins and assorted gen Z Gallaghers in attendance, then making it available to buy immediately, with half of the pieces under £50. Topshop relaunched last year and now has concessions in 30 John Lewis stores, as well as the luxury retailer Liberty.

Lisa Illis, the head of design at M&S, describes their recent catwalk show as “making the buzz of London fashion week accessible to everyone”. She says “more fashion-informed seasonal collections” have seen the number of under-35s shopping at the retailer increase 16% year on year.

The Hollywood stylist Law Roach, whose clients include Zendaya, has been appointed stylist-in-residence at Asos, where his influence will be felt not just in advertising campaigns, but also through his suggestions on different items from across the site to wear together.
points: Gap, M&S, Topshop and more are taking a leaf from luxury label playbooks to satisfy savvier generation of shoppers.

articles.title: Is AI your new wingman? How chatbots are transforming dating
articles.summary: Almost 40% of British singles have used AI for romantic advice, from writing messages to assessing potential partners. After Sam’s ex joked that her sister found him ugly, he turned to AI. Google Gemini had a look at the photo and politely disagreed.
body: The 27-year-old from Stoke-on-Trent is not the only AI-assisted romantic – a survey of 3,000 British singles published this month by Match Group, the owner of the Tinder and Hinge platforms, found 39% had used AI in their dating lives.

Relying on AI is bad, Sam tells the Guardian, adding he would rather begin dating in person, but there is a “paradigm shift in dating that’s occurring, which is really odd, where everything is expected to start online”.

The proportion of AI use in dating is even higher for younger generations, rising to 66% for members of gen Z (people born in the mid 1990s to early 2010s), and 53% of millennials (those born in the early 1980s to mid-90s).

Sam says pressure to make a good impression on dating apps means a misunderstood message could risk him losing out on dates. “Online dating … as a guy it’s a bit of a ghost town,” he says. “Rather than saying: ‘Hey, how’s your weekend going?’ it’s thinking about what I can pick up that might get a response.”

articles.title: ‘A gust of wind blowing back her hair added something special’: Mark McEvoy’s best phone picture
articles.summary: It was very cold and the young smoker was barelegged, barefoot and wearing a fur coat … How could the photographer resist? This Margate shop is now an ice-cream parlour, but back in 2014 it was a vintage clothes store.
body: “I remember it being a very cold October day, so I was surprised she was barelegged and barefoot,” he says. “My guess is that she was working in the shop, or maybe a friend of someone working there. The fur coat may even have been for sale inside, just something she put on to keep warm during a cigarette break.”
McEvoy didn’t notice the blond-haired, barelegged mannequin in the window until he stepped back. “A gust of wind blowing back her hair and her pose added something special,” he notes.

In more recent years, McEvoy has been scanning and collating his 40-year archive of photographs, and reflecting on his work across various devices and formats; a range of iPhone models but also analogue cameras, both 35mm and medium format. “I am a bit of a purist, inspired by the documentary tradition of cropping in the frame when you take the photo. So, rather than say to myself, ‘I can crop that out in post’, I’ll move physically closer to the subject instead,” McEvoy says.

articles.title: ‘We’re looking at a 30-year run’: UK pair aim to complete world’s most complex board game
articles.summary: Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa. “We have had a six-turn practice run. It took about 18 months,” said Andy Taeger, with what seemed like a chuckle as he contemplated playing the world’s most complicated board game.
body: “Based on that, we are looking at a 20- to 30-year run for the full game,” said his gaming partner James Purcell. “We’ve come to terms with it.”
The Guardian joined the pair in a Newcastle front room on Friday as they prepared to start an insane odyssey, playing the legendarily knotty war game The Campaign for North Africa.

If they finish it – and that, subject to the events of the next two to three decades, is the intention – they will become the first people known to have completed a game so vast, detailed and time-consuming that it has achieved mythical status in board gaming communities. It is a holy grail.

Purcell, 29, is a mental health worker from Wallsend, Taeger, 30, a software developer from Gosforth. They’re happy to be called geeks. They met about 10 years ago and realised straight away that they had a connection.
points: Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa.

articles.title: Gigi Hadid Cut the Ribbon on Her Fourth Guest in Residence Store with Cashmere, Caviar, and Caricatures
articles.summary: Model and founder Gigi Hadid, clad in a shrunken top and tartan skirt, celebrated the debut of her label’s fourth U.S. store—and its very first uptown address.
body: The first surprise was a trio of pretzels twisted into the letters G, I, and R at the entrance. Inside, florists busied themselves preparing custom arrangements, a three-piece band played beneath a sloped skylight, and a caricature artist stationed near the bar had guests voguing for their portraits and later comparing their likenesses.

Martini glasses were filled with one of two things: martinis, of course, but also cigarettes. Meanwhile, caviar in every conceivable configuration made the rounds: atop passed blinis, with potato chips and crème fraîche at a help-yourself station, and even crowning freshly baked potatoes.

articles.title: This Iconic New England Hotel Is My Favorite Place to Stay During Fall Foliage Season
articles.summary: With sweeping views of the White Mountains, a heated outdoor pool, and fantastic leaf-peeping, this historic grand hotel keeps drawing me back.
body: Welcome to Rebooked, Condé Nast Traveler's column where we share the properties our editors and contributors loved so much, they’ve booked them over and over (and over!) again. Travel journalists have their pick of the litter—so you know these are something special.

Every fall, I make the drive from New York City to New Hampshire ’s White Mountains. It’s my favorite place to see colorful foliage, and the long drive is well worth it for the symphony of red, orange, and yellow that swathes the mountains each autumn. The winding roads, narrow mountain passes, and charming New England towns along the way make the journey feel less like a trek and more like part of the vacation. At the end of the nearly six-hour drive, in the village called Bretton Woods, awaits the grand, historic Omni Mount Washington Resort, a hotel I've been visiting since I was a kid.

One of the things I love most about the Omni Mount Washington is how much there is to do. Between two golf courses, the Bretton Woods Ski Area (which offers scenic gondola rides in the fall), guided hikes, fly-fishing, horseback riding, and a 25,000-square-foot spa, you could fill an entire week without venturing off the property.
points: With sweeping views of the White Mountains, a heated outdoor pool, and fantastic leaf-peeping, this historic grand hotel keeps drawing me back.

articles.summary: If you’re in a bind this Halloween, chances are you can pull together a costume straight from your closet, using these street style looks as inspiration.

To wit: a white gown from Wiederhoft or Simone Rocha could instantly transform you into a bride on October 31st, while Jonathan Anderson’s fall 2026 menswear show will help you channel your inner rock star.

For those celebrating All Hallow’s Eve at Madison Square Garden, a Harry Styles costume topped off with a pair of colorful Adidas sneakers is the comfiest way to dance the night away. An orange and blue ensemble, on the other hand, will allow you to support our favorite hometown team (the New York Knicks, of course!). Turns out if you look hard enough, everything can double as a Halloween costume. Talk about cost per wear! Should you need a little inspo, we’ve pulled some fab ideas from our deep archive of street style, which only proves you can dress up in costume and still look smashing. articles.title: Toxic Friendship: How to Spot One—and What to Do About It
articles.summary: Wondering if you're in a toxic friendship? Experts reveal the warning signs, how to set boundaries, when to walk away, and when the problem is actually you.
body: When Alexa met Amelia at an event, she felt an instant kinship. They had so much in common—they were both in their mid-30s, both working at wellness startups, and both reeling from recent breakups. They exchanged numbers and started texting immediately. Their first “date” was at a neighborhood wine bar where they sipped vermouth and commiserated about the terrible thrill of being single again. Soon after, they were hanging out all the time—pilates on Tuesday mornings, dinner on Friday nights, takeout in Alexa’s living room on hungover Sunday afternoons. “We were so alike and in such similar life stages; our friendship felt almost cosmically aligned,” Alexa says.

That is, until about a year in, when Alexa started to sense that something about their dynamic wasn’t quite right. For one, Amelia’s problems had started to dominate their conversations—how much she hated her new boss, how she thought her new apartment was a dump, how frustrated she was that yet another guy she liked hadn’t texted her back. It seemed like her grievances were all they ever talked about now.
points: Experts reveal the warning signs, how to set boundaries, when to walk away, and when the problem is actually you.
